item.title: Retirement Plans: Identifying Ways to Help Mitigate Employer Risks Is Key to Continuing Defined Benefit Plans
item.description:
What GAO Found
Defined Benefit (DB) plan coverage has declined over the last nearly 5 decades. In 1975, about 27 percent of private-sector workers participated in a single-employer DB plan. By 2023, that number had decreased to about 5 percent. Stakeholders cited a complex range of factors that contributed to this decline including increased costs, financial volatility for employers, and changes in the labor market, such as the decline of unions that often negotiated for DB benefits.
Percentage of Private-Sector Workers Participating in Single-Employer DB Plans Sponsored by Their Current Employer, 1975–2023
Even in light of the steep decline, part of the Pension Benefit Guarantee Corporation’s (PBGC) mission is to encourage the continuation of DB plans. Stakeholders suggested PBGC take a proactive role in providing information about DB plan designs that use risk-sharing features between employers and workers, but it has not done so to date. Such designs may allow employers to mitigate risks and continue offering DB plans instead of terminating them or closing them to new participants. According to PBGC officials, they are waiting for newly collected data on some risk-sharing plan designs before publishing information on them. Nevertheless, while PBGC awaits new data, it has the opportunity to assess how its resources and expertise can help meet stakeholders’ information needs.
Stakeholders knowledgeable about the pension models GAO reviewed in the U.S. and other countries described risk-sharing strategies to help limit the financial risks employers face when offering a DB plan. For example, plans could allow limited adjustments to retirement benefits to alleviate some of the risks associated with paying lifelong benefits. The stakeholders noted that plan sponsors would make stable, predictable contributions, and participants would receive lifetime income with limited adjustments to address financial shortfalls due to factors such as investment performance.
Stakeholders identified various policy options that could promote private-sector DB plans by reducing the cost and administrative burden of maintaining an existing DB plan. For example, stakeholders said modernized plan designs or reformed PBGC premiums could reduce the cost of maintaining a DB plan and help some plan sponsors overcome challenges.
Why GAO Did This Study
DB retirement plans provide secure retirement income for millions of retirees and their families and help employers retain employees. However, the portion of the private-sector workforce covered by these plans has declined for decades. This decline has caused concern about retirees’ ability to secure an adequate standard of living. As fewer workers are covered by DB plans, more retirees may rely on Social Security as their only source of guaranteed retirement income.
GAO was asked to review trends in DB plan coverage and options to help sustain or expand that coverage. This report examines (1) trends in coverage, (2) PBGC’s efforts to encourage DB plans to continue, (3) strategies used in the U.S. and abroad to modernize plan design, and (4) policy options to expand DB plan coverage.
GAO reviewed relevant literature and interviewed agency officials and 22 subject matter specialists, including actuaries, researchers, and industry groups. GAO also analyzed data from the Department of Labor and PBGC, as well as data on historical interest and mortality rates. GAO reviewed agency publications and interviewed officials. GAO also reviewed documentation on four DB plans used in other countries and interviewed knowledgeable stakeholders and officials about these plans, which were selected to represent a variety of plan design options. To identify policy options, GAO interviewed the subject matter specialists and reviewed relevant literature.
